nameStory: The yellow-fringed dolichomia gets its name from the delicate yellow fringe along the edges of its wings, which gives it a decorative, almost lace-like appearance. The name 'dolichomia' comes from Greek words meaning 'long' and 'thread,' possibly referring to the moth's slender antennae or thread-like wing patterns that help distinguish it from other small moths.
description: The yellow-fringed dolichomia is a small, delicate moth in the snout moth family, easily recognized by its distinctive yellow wing fringes. With a wingspan of just 16-24 millimeters (about the size of a large coin), this petite moth has brownish wings accented by bright yellow edges that catch the light beautifully. Like other snout moths, it has a prominent 'snout' formed by extended mouthparts that project forward from its head. Despite its small size, the contrasting colors make it quite noticeable when it's active around lights or resting on tree bark.

idTips.label: Yellow wing fringes
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive bright yellow fringe along the outer edges of both forewings and hindwings - this golden trim is the moth's signature feature and easily visible even in dim light

idTips.label: Small size
idTips.description: Tiny wingspan of 16-24mm makes it about the size of a nickel or quarter when wings are spread - much smaller than most moths you'll encounter

idTips.label: Snout projection
idTips.description: Extended mouthparts form a noticeable 'snout' that projects forward from the head like a tiny elephant trunk - feels rigid if gently touched

idTips.label: Brown wing coloration
idTips.description: Wings appear mottled brown to grayish-brown with subtle patterns, providing good camouflage against tree bark when at rest

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: When at rest, holds wings in a triangular tent-like position over its body rather than spread flat, creating a distinctive peaked silhouette

habitat: Found throughout New England's oak forests and woodlands, as the larvae depend entirely on oak trees (Quercus species) for food. Look for adults around white oak, red oak, and other native oak species, particularly in mixed hardwood forests and oak-dominated areas. They're often spotted near outdoor lights in suburban areas with mature oak trees, and can be found from sea level to moderate elevations throughout the region.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in May, often seen flying around outdoor lights on warm evenings. Look for them resting on oak bark during the day.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period through June and July, with moths most active on warm, humid nights. This is the best time to spot them at porch lights or near oak groves.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into August in northern New England, though numbers decline. Late-season individuals may appear slightly worn with less vibrant yellow fringes.
seasonality.winter: Adults are not active; the species overwinters in an earlier life stage. No moths to be found during cold months.

funFact: Despite being called a 'snout moth,' the yellow-fringed dolichomia's prominent snout isn't used for piercing or biting - instead, it houses a coiled-up tongue that works like a tiny garden hose to sip nectar from flowers, and the snout can actually be longer than the moth's entire head!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other small brown moths, but the bright yellow wing fringes are a dead giveaway - no other common New England moth has this distinctive golden trim. Remember: 'Yellow edges = yellow-fringed dolichomia.'
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'Pyralidae' comes from the Greek word for 'fire,' as many snout moths in this family are attracted to flames and lights. This attraction to artificial lights can make them seem more common in suburban areas than they actually are in wild habitats.
compareHints: As the only Hypsopygia species recorded in New England, it's most similar to other small snout moths in the Pyralidae family. However, most other snout moths lack the distinctive yellow wing fringes and tend to be either larger or have different color patterns. The combination of small size, prominent snout, and yellow-fringed wings makes this species quite distinctive among New England's snout moths.
